blocks.text: Quick verdict

FloppyData is the cheaper choice: $10 for 10 GB against $40 at Infatica, and $100 for 100 GB against $360, with residential, mobile and datacenter traffic on one balance. Infatica is the better choice when you need ZIP-level targeting, IPv6 residential IPs, a fully featured trial, or sourcing documentation and ISO certifications for procurement, and it has a longer independent testing record. Budget experiments suit FloppyData; compliance-sensitive or location-precise work suits Infatica.

FloppyData and Infatica both sell residential, mobile, datacenter and static IPs, but they sell very different promises. FloppyData promises simplicity and price: a flat $1/GB on one balance. Infatica promises precision and assurance: ZIP targeting on every plan, a written no-reselling policy, ISO certifications and a $4 seven-day trial. This comparison helps you decide whether the savings from FloppyData outweigh the confidence Infatica offers.

blocks.text: FloppyData in 2026: what you get

FloppyData is a young budget provider registered in Dubai that launched around 2024. Its pitch is radical simplicity: one balance at a flat $1/GB that you can spend on residential, mobile or datacenter rotating traffic, plus static residential and datacenter IPs sold in monthly bundles. Its residential page lists home ISP IPs in 148 countries and 442 cities. The company also offers a free cloud anti-detect browser that runs on its proxies. Its advertised 65M+ IP figure has been questioned by some reviewers, and user reviews are mixed.

Strengths: Flat $1/GB on any volume; One balance across residential, mobile and datacenter; Cheap static residential bundles with unlimited bandwidth; Free cloud anti-detect browser. Weak spots: Newer brand with limited independent testing; Pool-size claims disputed by some reviewers; Mixed customer-support reviews.
Infatica in 2026: what you get

Infatica pitches itself on ethical sourcing and features available to every customer. All residential plans include country, city and ZIP targeting, IP whitelisting and selectable rotation times, and a 7-day $4 trial lowers the risk of testing. Independent reviewers have found its proxies fast and its pool modest but respectable. Its niche extra is a premium IPv6 residential pool, rare in this market, at about 1.5x the normal per-GB price.

Strengths: ZIP targeting included on every plan; Clear sourcing policy and ISO certifications; Cheap 7-day trial; Rare IPv6 residential pool. Weak spots: Mid-range pool size; Per-GB price stays above $3.50 until large volumes; Subscription traffic does not roll over.
Pricing: FloppyData vs Infatica

FloppyData charges a flat $1/GB for rotating traffic, and the same balance works for residential, mobile and datacenter IPs. Static residential proxies are sold in monthly bundles from $1.79 per IP (20 IPs for $49), and static datacenter IPs from $0.79 per IP.

Infatica charges $4/GB pay-as-you-go for residential traffic. Subscriptions cost $3.84/GB at 25 GB, $3.60/GB at 100 GB, and fall to about $2.70/GB at 500 GB and $2.60/GB at 1 TB. Premium IPv6 residential runs at roughly 1.5x those rates, starting at $6/GB.

At 10 GB a month, FloppyData is the cheaper option at about $10 against $40 for Infatica, roughly 75% less. For a 100 GB month, FloppyData costs about $100 while Infatica costs about $360, so FloppyData saves around 72%. Both FloppyData and Infatica work on allowances that do not carry forward indefinitely, so size your plan to real monthly usage rather than buying ahead.
Pool size, coverage and targeting

FloppyData does not publish a clear residential pool figure, so a size comparison is not possible on published data. FloppyData lists '65M+ claimed (disputed)' and Infatica lists '35M-40M'. In practice, what matters is how many unique IPs you get in the countries you target, which you can measure in a short trial by sending a few thousand requests and counting distinct exit addresses. For coverage, FloppyData lists 148 (residential) countries and Infatica lists 195. On targeting, FloppyData offers country and city, while Infatica offers country, state, city and ZIP.
Protocols, sessions and setup

Both providers support SOCKS5 as well as HTTP(S), so either will plug into scrapers, anti-detect browsers and automation tools that expect a SOCKS endpoint. On sessions, FloppyData offers rotating or sticky sessions, and Infatica offers per-request rotation or selectable rotation times. Both use a backconnect gateway: you point your tool at one host and port, and choose country, city or session behaviour through parameters in the username.
Which is better for your use case?

General web scraping: Infatica. Infatica has the edge here. Why: fast proxies that did well on popular targets in independent tests. How FloppyData compares: cheap, but with limited independent benchmarking.
SERP and rank tracking: Infatica. Infatica has the edge here. Why: ZIP targeting helps local search results. How FloppyData compares: workable for light tasks.

Social media and multi-account management: FloppyData wins. The deciding factor for FloppyData: cheap static residential IPs and a free anti-detect browser. The limitation on the Infatica side: rotation controls are good but very long sticky sessions are not a headline feature.
E-commerce price and stock monitoring: Infatica. Infatica has the edge here. Why: ZIP-level targeting for local prices. How FloppyData compares: city targeting at a flat rate.
Ad verification and geo-testing: Infatica. Infatica has the edge here. Why: precise geo targeting and clean sourcing. How FloppyData compares: limited targeting depth and published data.
Tight budgets: FloppyData wins. The deciding factor for FloppyData: a flat $1/GB on any volume. The limitation on the Infatica side: mid-range pricing until you reach large volumes.
Trials, verification and billing fine print

Before you pay, check how each provider lets you test. FloppyData: No free trial; free browser extension for testing a few locations. Infatica: 7-day trial for $4 (residential) or $8 (mobile). Verification and payment rules differ too. FloppyData: Light. Infatica: Standard verification; states it does not resell IPs. Whichever you choose, measure cost per successful request rather than cost per gigabyte: retries, blocked pages and heavy page assets all burn bandwidth, and a cheaper network that fails more often can end up costing more. Blocking images and fonts in your scraper, reusing sessions where a target allows it, and capping concurrency are the quickest ways to cut the bill on either provider.
How to test FloppyData and Infatica before you commit
The quickest way to choose between FloppyData and Infatica is a side-by-side test on the sites and countries you actually care about:
1. Buy the smallest option on each side (FloppyData: no free trial; free browser extension for testing a few locations; Infatica: 7-day trial for $4 (residential) or $8 (mobile)).
2. Pick three to five real target URLs and the two or three countries that matter most, and send the same number of requests (a few hundred is enough) through each provider at the same time of day.
3. Record success rate, median response time, CAPTCHAs or blocks, and the number of unique exit IPs you received per country.
4. Divide what you spent by the number of successful, correctly located responses to get cost per useful request, then scale that to your monthly volume.
Bottom line

Across the six use cases above, FloppyData comes out ahead in 2, Infatica in 4, and 0 are ties. That makes Infatica the safer default if you are unsure, but the right answer still depends on your volume and targets: FloppyData is strongest for small budgets and experiments, while Infatica is strongest for compliance-conscious buyers. If you can, spend a few dollars testing both on the exact sites and countries you care about; a one-hour test tells you more than any spec sheet.
